lead: Distributorless ignition removes the rotating distributor and gives each coil its own cylinders. In the waste-spark form one coil serves a pair of cylinders and fires both plugs together: one plug is near the end of compression and lights the charge, the other is on its exhaust stroke and the spark is wasted. Direct ignition goes further: one coil per cylinder, on or near the plug, fired only on compression. The ECU times every spark from crank and cam sensors. Only a few universities teach this as a separate topic; it extends electronic and programmed ignition.

blocks.text: Waste spark uses one double-ended coil for two cylinders whose pistons rise and fall together but are 360° apart in the cycle. In a four-cylinder engine with firing order 1-3-4-2 the pairs are 1 & 4 and 2 & 3. The two ends of the secondary go to the two plugs, and the current runs from one plug to earth, through the block, and back up through the other plug, so the two sparks are in series and of opposite polarity.

When cylinder 1 is near the end of compression, cylinder 4 is near the end of exhaust. The compressed gas in cylinder 1 needs most of the voltage; the hot, low-pressure exhaust gas in cylinder 4 breaks down at only a few kilovolts. One revolution later the roles swap. So each coil fires once every crank revolution, twice in the 720° cycle, and the ECU needs only the crank sensor: a spark on every revolution always lands on the right stroke of one of the two cylinders.

Waste spark needs no cap, rotor or long leads, so it is cheap and common on small engines. Its costs are a plug that sparks twice as often, so it wears faster, and timing that can be trimmed only pair by pair.

sections.h3: Direct ignition: one coil per cylinder

blocks.text: Direct ignition gives every cylinder its own coil, mounted on the plug (coil-on-plug) or close to it with a short lead (coil-near-plug). The ECU fires each coil only on its compression stroke. A crank sensor reading a trigger wheel gives speed and angle; a missing tooth marks a reference position. But one crank revolution looks exactly like the next, so the crank alone cannot tell compression from exhaust. A cam sensor, turning at half crank speed, gives one pulse per 720° and tells the ECU which revolution it is in. That is why direct ignition needs a cam sensor and waste spark does not.

The high-voltage path is a few centimetres long, so lead losses and radio interference fall. Each cylinder's timing can be trimmed by its own knock signal, and a coil has a whole cycle to recharge, so dwell is never short. Many coils are "smart coils" with the igniter built in, triggered by a low-voltage signal from the ECU.

There is no rotor to burn, cap to track, or distributor shaft play to upset timing, and the timing cannot be adjusted by hand. A misfire on one cylinder of a direct system points to that cylinder's coil, plug or boot; a misfire on both cylinders of a pair on a waste-spark engine points to the shared coil. The ECU watches crank speed for the small slow-down after a dead cylinder, and some ECUs check the coil's primary current, to name the cylinder in a fault code. Keep the plug gap correct: a wide gap raises the voltage demand and can cause flashover inside a worn coil boot.

examples.question: A four-cylinder engine with firing order 1-3-4-2 runs at 4000 rpm on waste spark, with coils paired 1 & 4 and 2 & 3. Find the length of one cycle, the firings per second of each coil, the useful sparks per second, and the crank angle of each firing with the cylinder on compression.
steps: Speed = 4000 ÷ 60 = 66.67 rev/s. One 720° cycle is 2 revolutions, so it lasts 2 ÷ 66.67 = 0.030 s = 30 ms.
Each coil fires once per revolution, so 66.67 firings per second per coil, 133.3 for the two coils together.
Each firing gives one useful spark (compression) and one wasted spark (exhaust), so the engine gets 133.3 useful sparks per second, and every plug sparks 66.67 times per second.
The cylinders fire 180° apart in the order 1-3-4-2: cylinder 1 at 0°, 3 at 180°, 4 at 360°, 2 at 540°.

Coil 1 & 4 fires at 0° (1 on compression, 4 on exhaust) and 360° (4 on compression, 1 on exhaust); coil 2 & 3 fires at 180° (3 compression) and 540° (2 compression). The firings are 180° × 30 ms/720° = 7.5 ms apart.
examples.answer: Cycle 30 ms; 66.7 firings per second per coil; 133.3 useful sparks per second; firings every 7.5 ms at 0° (cylinder 1), 180° (3), 360° (4) and 540° (2).

traps: Saying a waste-spark coil fires once per cycle. It fires once every revolution, twice per 720°, and each firing sparks both of its plugs.
Thinking direct ignition can run on the crank sensor alone. It needs the cam sensor to tell compression from exhaust; waste spark does not.
Pairing cylinders by neighbouring numbers. Pair the cylinders whose pistons move together and are 360° apart in the firing order: 1 & 4, 2 & 3.
Forgetting that the two waste-spark plugs are in series and of opposite polarity; the exhaust-stroke plug takes only a few kilovolts.
Calling coil-near-plug the same as coil-on-plug; coil-near-plug keeps a short high-voltage lead.

quiz.a: Both plugs of a paired coil fire together; one spark is at the end of compression and lights the charge, the other is at the end of exhaust and does nothing.

quiz.q: Why does direct ignition need a cam sensor?
quiz.a: The crank sensor gives angle within one revolution, but two revolutions look the same. The cam turns once per 720° and tells the ECU which revolution has compression, so each coil fires only on its compression stroke.

quiz.q: A four-cylinder waste-spark engine runs at 6000 rpm. Find the firings per second of each coil.
quiz.a: 6000 rpm = 100 rev/s and each coil fires once per revolution, so 100 firings per second per coil (200 for the engine, half of them useful).

quiz.q: Compare waste spark and coil-on-plug for timing accuracy and cost.
quiz.a: Coil-on-plug fires only on compression, recharges for a whole cycle and lets the ECU trim each cylinder by its own knock signal, at the cost of one coil per cylinder and a cam sensor. Waste spark uses half the coils and no cam sensor, but wears plugs twice as fast and trims timing only pair by pair.

quiz.q: Name the two forms of distributorless ignition.
quiz.a: Waste spark (one double-ended coil per pair of cylinders) and direct ignition (one coil per cylinder, coil-on-plug or coil-near-plug). Both are static ignition: the high voltage is shared out without moving parts.

quiz.q: What does a missing tooth on a trigger wheel provide?
quiz.a: A reference mark: the longer gap tells the ECU a known crank position, from which it counts teeth to find every spark angle.

quiz.q: Firing order 1-3-4-2, coil 1 & 4 fires at 0°. Give the next three firings and the cylinder on compression at each.
quiz.a: 180°: coil 2 & 3, cylinder 3; 360°: coil 1 & 4, cylinder 4; 540°: coil 2 & 3, cylinder 2.

beyond: Coil-on-plug units now carry their own igniter and sometimes ion-current sensing, so the plug reports knock and misfire after each spark. Higher-voltage coils serve lean-burn and high-boost engines. Search terms: coil-on-plug, smart coil, ion current sensing, static ignition.
